title: What the Federal Reserve Actually Is — Structure, Need, and the Compromise

record: It's neither. It's a documented, real hybrid: twelve regional Reserve Banks privately owned by their member banks, overseen by a public, Senate-confirmed Board of Governors. It was created specifically because the US suffered a banking panic roughly every fifteen years for decades, with no institution able to stop one — and in 1907, the closest thing to a backstop was one private banker's personal fortune. Congress built something else specifically so that would never be the plan again.

record: SIPRI's own strict threshold counts exactly three qualifying state suppliers of complete major weapons systems — but SIPRI explicitly states many more countries supply components, ammunition, and services outside that narrow category. title: The International Legal and Political Context

The ICC's November 2024 arrest warrants charge war crimes and crimes against humanity specifically, not genocide. Both are real, significant, documented legal proceedings; neither is the final genocide determination popular shorthand sometimes implies.

title: Is This Unprecedented, or Does It Fit a Pattern?
told: Israel's arms suppliers face an unprecedented dilemma — there's no real precedent for weighing a close ally's conduct against documented humanitarian and legal concerns.
record: There is real precedent, and it's instructive: a unanimous, binding UN arms embargo has been imposed on a state with Western allies' backing before (South Africa, 1977, with US/UK/French votes in favor). Sweeping Western sanctions have been imposed on a veto-holding power before (Russia, 2022). And the closest real analogy — a documented Western ally accused of serious international law violations (Saudi Arabia, Yemen) — produced a real but partial, contested, and substantially reversed response, not a clean embargo.

title: How This Relationship Gets Maintained Politically — By Country

This is ordinary, legally regulated, traceable political activity — not one hidden operation.

title: The Ethics in Government Act
told: After Watergate, Congress permanently fixed the problem — an independent mechanism now exists that cannot be politically controlled.

chapter_name: Power Protects Power — The DOJ Architecture
title: The Iran-Contra Pardons

A reform built to constrain one mechanism left a different, older mechanism completely intact.

chapter_name: Power Protects Power — The DOJ Architecture

title: Taxation

record: Israel's top bracket (50%) is higher than the US federal top rate (37%), but Israel's bottom brackets are gentler in absolute terms, and the US adds state income tax on top in most states, which narrows or reverses the gap depending on the state.

title: Cost of Living

title: Jobs, Wages & the Safety Net

A message sent to a listener who has unsubscribed produces exactly nothing, which is what the record shows.

title: Zionism's Origins, and Palestine Before 1948
told: Israel and its conflicts in the region trace back to an ancient, continuous national presence with no meaningful break.
record: Zionism was founded as an organized political movement in 1897 at the First Zionist Congress in Basel, Switzerland, by Theodor Herzl, an Austro-Hungarian journalist — its founding leadership was overwhelmingly European, and its stated goal, per the Congress's own Basel Program, was "a home for the Jewish people to be secured under public law" in Ottoman-ruled Palestine. Palestine, as a place with an Arab-majority population, existed under Ottoman and then British administration for the half-century before 1948 — this is simply the documented state of the territory in the decades this module's

title: Independence, War, and Lebanon's Own Declaration
told: Israel's 1948 war with Lebanon was purely a matter of Israeli aggression against a neutral neighboring state.
record: Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948; the next day, Egypt, Syria, Jordan, Iraq, and Lebanon — Lebanon among them, by its own government's decision — declared war and invaded. Lebanon fielded the smallest of the five Arab armies; Israeli forces repelled the invasion and temporarily occupied part of southern Lebanon before an armistice was signed March 23, 1949, restoring the internationally recognized border. In the same conflict, roughly 100,000-110,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were displaced into Lebanon.

title: Fatah's Attacks, and the Six-Day War
told: Armed conflict along the Israel-Lebanon border began only after Israel's 1967 territorial gains.

The June 1967 war, in which Israel decisively defeated Egypt, Syria, and Jordan in six days, produced a second wave of Palestinian displacement (the "Naksa") and sent thousands more refugees into Lebanon; a year later, Arafat's Fatah took control of the PLO.

title: The Cairo Agreement, and the PLO's Relocation to Lebanon

title: The Verdun Raid, and the Slide Into Civil War

Two years later, on April 13, 1975, Christian Phalangist gunmen attacked a bus carrying Palestinians in the Beirut suburb of Ain al-Rummaneh, following an earlier assassination attempt against Phalange leader Pierre Gemayel — a purely Lebanese sectarian incident, with no Israeli involvement, that is conventionally dated as the start of Lebanon's 1975-1990 civi

title: Operation Litani and UN Resolution 425
told: UN Security Council resolutions on this conflict have gone consistently unenforced with no documented international response mechanism.
record: In March 1978, following continued PLO cross-border raids, Israel invaded Lebanon and advanced to the Litani River. The UN Security Council responded immediately with Resolution 425, demanding Israel's immediate withdrawal and establishing UNIFIL (the UN Interim Force in Lebanon), which continues operating to this day. In the same period, Israel began arming and financing the South Lebanon Army (SLA), a militia composed of Lebanese Christians.

title: The Invasion, the Siege of Beirut, and the PLO's Expulsion
told: Israel's 1982 invasion was a narrowly-scoped border security operation that unintentionally expanded.
record: On June 6, 1982, roughly 60,000 Israeli soldiers crossed into Lebanon under Defense Minister Ariel Sharon in an operation publicly named "Peace for Galilee," reaching and laying siege to Beirut — far beyond the announced security-buffer objective. The PLO, besieged in West Beirut, was forced to evacuate to Tunis under multinational peacekeeping supervision on August 30-September 1, 1982. Lebanese Forces leader and President-elect Bashir Gemayel was assassinated September 14 by a member of the Syrian Social Nationalist Party — setting the stage for the massacre documented in the next scene.

title: Sabra and Shatila: Two Official Findings, Not One
told: The Sabra and Shatila massacre was investigated once, conclusively, with a single agreed international finding.
record: On September 16-18, 1982, Lebanese Forces militiamen — allied with Israel and operating in a zone under Israeli military control — killed an estimated 800-3,500 Palestinian and Lebanese Shia civilians in the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps. Israel's own Kahan Commission (chaired by Israeli Supreme Court President Yitzhak Kahan) found the Phalangists directly responsible and Israel "indirectly responsible" for not foreseeing and preventing the violence, leading to Defense Minister Sharon's resignation. title: The Founding of Hezbollah
told: Hezbollah is simply an extension of general Lebanese Shia political sentiment with no distinct organizational origin.
record: Hezbollah formed in 1982 directly in response to Israel's invasion and subsequent occupation of southern Lebanon, organized and trained with the backing of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) — a documented foreign state sponsorship relationship from the organization's founding. Per Hilal Khashan, "Iran claimed responsibility for the Palestinian [cause] at a time when Arab countries had abandoned it," filling a sponsorship role the PLO's Arab state backers had increasingly stepped back from after 1970 and 1982.

title: The Security Zone, the SLA, and Two Named Operations
told: Israel's presence in southern Lebanon after 1985 was a stable, uncontested security arrangement.
record: After 1985, Israel withdrew most forces to a self-declared "security zone" along the Litani River in South Lebanon, maintained with the South Lebanon Army documented in Scene 7, continuing for 15 more years. Israel launched Operation Accountability in 1993 (after Hezbollah attacks killed at least five Israeli soldiers) and Operation Grapes of Wrath in 1996, the latter resulting in the Qana Massacre — an Israeli strike on a UN compound sheltering civilians that killed over 100 Lebanese people, including at least 37 children.

title: Israeli Withdrawal to the Blue Line
told: Israel maintained a permanent, unresolved military presence inside Lebanon from 1978 onward with no significant withdrawal.
record: On May 24, 2000, Israel announced and executed a full withdrawal to the "Blue Line" — the UN-demarcated international border — ending Israel's 22-year military presence in Lebanon documented since 1978. The UN certified the withdrawal as complete. Lebanon marks May 25 as a national holiday (Liberation Day) to this day. As Israeli forces withdrew, many South Lebanon Army members — the Israeli-backed militia documented in Scene 7 — fled with them, unable to remain safely in Lebanon.

title: The July War
told: The 2006 war began with an unprovoked Israeli invasion of Lebanon.
record: On July 12, 2006, Hezbollah crossed into Israeli territory, killed three soldiers, and captured two others, demanding a prisoner exchange — a specific, documented, named trigger for the war that followed. Israel responded with airstrikes and a ground campaign; Hezbollah launched rockets into northern Israel. The 34-day war (the "July War") killed approximately 1,200 Lebanese people, mostly civilians, and 158 Israelis, mostly soldiers — a casualty ratio of roughly 8-to-1. told: No significant activity occurred along the Israel-Lebanon border between 2006 and 2023.

In the same period, Israel violated Lebanese airspace more than 22,000 times between 2007 and 2022, per documented tracking — a sustained, large-scale practice occurring throughout a period otherwise characterized as calm.

title: October 7, Hezbollah's Solidarity Front, and the 2024 War

record: Hezbollah began firing on Israel on October 8, 2023, in what it termed solidarity with Hamas following Hamas's October 7 attack on Israel; low-intensity exchanges continued for nearly a year. On September 17, 2023 [2024], thousands of Hezbollah members' pagers and radios exploded simultaneously in a covert Israeli operation; Israel then launched intensive airstrikes (September 23), assassinated Hezbollah's longtime leader Hassan Nasrallah (September 27), and began a ground invasion (October 1). A ceasefire took effect November 27, 2024.

Perpetrators included Iraqi soldiers and police who had supported the collapsed coup, plus civilian mobs and Bedouin from the city's outskirts.

This had no Israel dimension at its origin; the UN Security Council authorized the coalition response under international law regarding the invasion of a sovereign state. told: Israel only acts against proven threats.
record: In plain terms: a preemptive strike destroys a thing for what it might become, not what it is. In code, that's calling dealloc on an object that hasn't finished initializing — a move the runtime never does on its own, because the decision to end a life belongs to the system, not to any one caller.

After Husni al-Za'im seized power in March 1949, armistice talks opened on April 5, and Za'im offered a peace treaty and military cooperation, proposed meeting Ben-Gurion or Moshe Sharett, and offered to resettle 250,000–300,000 Palestinian refugees in Syria, with the border drawn through the middle of Lake Hula and the Sea of Galilee . In a 1953–54 meeting recorded by the State Department, Israel's Moshe Dayan said Israel claimed sovereignty over Jewish lands in the zones and that 'someone must keep the area alive,' and that Israel did not want Syria to have direct access to the Jordan River . Syria fired on Israeli farmers and fishermen from the heights; Israel sent armored tractors to cultivate disputed land and conducted reprisal raids. title: June 1967 — The Golan Taken, Its People Displaced, Quneitra Destroyed
told: The Golan was an empty military plateau.
record: Israel captured the Golan on June 9–10, 1967. Estimates of the Syrian population that fled or was expelled range from roughly 80,000 to over 130,000; a few Druze villages in the north remained, and most other villages were razed in the following years . Under the 1974 disengagement Israel returned Quneitra, the main town, but before withdrawing its forces systematically demolished it; a UN special committee found the destruction deliberate, and the General Assembly condemned it . Syria left the ruins standing as a memorial.

chapter_name: Israel-Syria Architecture — From the 1949 Offer to the Sufa 53 Line
title: 1973 and Kissinger's Line — The Disengagement Agreement That Held for Fifty Years
told: Syria and Israel have been in constant fighting since 1967.
record: In October 1973 Syria briefly retook much of the Golan before Israel pushed beyond the 1967 line. The Agreement on Disengagement, signed May 31, 1974, separated the forces, returned Quneitra, allowed Syrian civilians to return to the buffer zone, and created the UN Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF); the text says it is 'not a peace agreement' but a step toward one under Resolution 338 . Despite no peace treaty, the Golan front became one of Israel's quietest for decades.

chapter_name: Israel-Syria Architecture — From the 1949 Offer to the Sufa 53 Line
title: December 1981 — Israel Annexes the Golan; the Security Council Says It Is 'Null and Void'
told: The Golan was lawfully annexed and the world accepted it.
record: The Golan Heights Law of December 14, 1981 applied Israeli law, jurisdiction and administration to the territory . On December 17, 1981 the Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 497, declaring the decision 'null and void and without international legal effect' and demanding that Israel rescind it; the United States voted in favor . Most of the Golan's Druze residents refused Israeli citizenship, staging a general strike in 1982 . Israeli settlement grew to tens of thousands of residents.

told: Syria never seriously negotiated with Israel.
record: Direct Israel–Syria negotiations began after the 1991 Madrid conference . Yitzhak Rabin conveyed through the US a conditional willingness to withdraw from the Golan for full peace and security arrangements — the so-called 'deposit' . Talks under Ehud Barak at Shepherdstown, West Virginia, in January 2000 produced a draft, and on March 26, 2000 Presidents Clinton and Hafez al-Assad met in Geneva; the effort collapsed over whether Syria's border would touch the northeastern shore of the Sea of Galilee — a strip of a few hundred meters . told: Syria never pursued nuclear capability.
record: In Operation Outside the Box, Israeli aircraft struck the al-Kibar site on September 6, 2007; the US later said it was a North Korean-designed reactor not declared to the IAEA, and the IAEA concluded it was very likely a reactor that should have been declared. Israel officially acknowledged the strike in March 2018 .

title: The War Years — Hundreds of Israeli Strikes, and Aid to Southern Rebels
told: Israel stayed entirely out of Syria's civil war.
record: From 2013 Israel struck weapons convoys, depots and Iranian-linked positions in Syria in what its military called the 'campaign between the wars'; former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot acknowledged thousands of strikes by early 2019 . Through 'Operation Good Neighbor' Israel treated thousands of wounded Syrians and delivered aid in the south; media investigations reported that it also supplied funds and some arms to rebel groups near the Golan, which Israel did not officially confirm in detail . Israel did not seek Assad's overthrow; its focus was Iran and Hezbollah.

title: Recognition by Proclamation — The US in 2019, Colombia in 2026, and Everyone Else
told: The world now accepts the Golan as Israel's.
record: On March 25, 2019 President Trump signed a proclamation recognizing the Golan Heights as part of Israel . In August 2026 Colombia recognized Israel's claim, according to reporting on Syria's UN address . The UN position under Resolution 497 is unchanged, and Syria's president told the General Assembly in September 2026 that the Golan 'will remain Syrian territory' .

title: December 8, 2024 — Assad Falls, Israel Moves In
told: Israel only defended its border after Assad's fall.
record: After Assad's fall on December 8, 2024, Israeli forces entered and occupied parts of the UNDOF buffer zone and areas beyond it, including the Syrian side of Mount Hermon, and carried out extensive airstrikes on Syrian military sites, aircraft, naval vessels and weapons stocks . Israel said the moves were temporary and defensive, to prevent weapons falling to hostile forces; Syria and the UN called them violations of the 1974 agreement.

title: 2025 — Sweida, Strikes on Damascus, and Talks in the Open
told: Post-Assad Syria and Israel have had no contact.
record: Al-Sharaa acknowledged direct security discussions with Israel; during a Washington visit he was asked about the Abraham Accords and did not commit to recognizing Israel . Israel conducted strikes in Syria through 2025, including in Damascus during deadly clashes in the Druze-majority province of Sweida in July, citing protection of the Druze community . Al-Sharaa later said Israel's demand for a broad buffer zone amounted to 'Israel's insistence on remaining on Syrian territory' .

chapter_name: Israel-Syria Architecture — From the 1949 Offer to the Sufa 53 Line
title: 2026 — '90% of a Deal,' 500 Strikes, and a Line Being Dug Into Syrian Soil
told: Israel's presence in southern Syria is temporary and winding down.
record: In July 2026 al-Sharaa said Syria was working toward a security agreement, involving several countries, that would see Israeli forces leave the buffer zone and could open the way to comprehensive peace, without relinquishing the Golan . In September he said talks had reached 'almost 90%' before Israel withdrew, and that October 7 'cannot dictate' Israel's Syria policy . At the UN General Assembly on September 23 he cited about 500 Israeli airstrikes, more than 1,200 incursions and 300 detentions, and called for withdrawal to the December 8, 2024 lines . In early October Syria accused Israel of

chapter_name: Israel-Syria Architecture — From the 1949 Offer to the Sufa 53 Line
title: The Machine in Code — A 'Temporary' Object Inside an Autorelease Pool That Never Drains
told: Temporary security measures end when the threat ends.
record: Plainly: a 'temporary' presence becomes permanent not by announcement but by accumulation — a summit held, a road built, a trench dug. Each step is small; together they change the map. That is an object retained inside a pool that was supposed to free it.

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: Ruled, Not Settled — Four Centuries of Ottoman Palestine, and the Treaty That Ended It
told: The Ottomans 'occupied' Palestine the way settlers later did, or Palestine was an empty Ottoman backwater.
record: From 1516 to 1917 (apart from Egyptian rule in 1831–40) Palestine was administered as Ottoman provinces, chiefly the district of Jerusalem and parts of the provinces of Beirut and Damascus, with no border separating it from today's Syria, Lebanon or Jordan (see 'Four Centuries Under One Roof'). Ottoman rule was imperial administration: governors, garrisons and taxation over a population that remained largely Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, with long-established Jewish communities. British forces captured Jerusalem in December 1917. The Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923, renounced all

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: The Sultan's 'No' — and the Ottoman Law That Opened the Door Anyway
told: The Ottoman Empire welcomed or sold Palestine to the Zionist movement.
record: Herzl sought a charter from the Sultan from 1896, offering to help consolidate the Ottoman public debt; his diary records a message relayed from Abdul Hamid II that he could not sell even a foot of the land because it belonged not to him but to his people . Herzl finally met the Sultan in May 1901 without obtaining a charter . From the 1880s the Ottoman government imposed restrictions on Jewish immigration and land purchase in Palestine, enforced unevenly and undermined by corruption and foreign consular protection. Meanwhile the Ottoman Land Code of 1858 required registration of land titles;

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: The First Muslim-Majority State to Recognize Israel — Then a Secret Pact, Then an Alliance
told: Turkey has always been hostile to Israel.
record: Turkey and Israel established diplomatic relations in March 1949 . In 1958 Turkey joined the secret 'Trident' intelligence alliance with Israel and Iran (see 'He Joined the Embargo'). In 1996 the two countries signed military-cooperation and defense-industry agreements covering training, exercises and arms upgrades; Israeli pilots trained in Turkish airspace, and Israeli firms modernized Turkish aircraft and tanks . Trade and tourism grew, and Turkish governments of the 1990s treated Israel as a strategic partner.

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: Erdoğan's Turn — Davos, and the Mavi Marmara
told: The rupture came from nowhere.
record: After the 2008–09 Gaza war Erdoğan confronted Shimon Peres at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January 2009 and left the stage. On May 31, 2010 Israeli forces boarded the Mavi Marmara, the lead ship of a flotilla seeking to break the Gaza blockade; nine activists were killed, one of them a dual Turkish-American citizen, and a tenth died later of his wounds . Israeli soldiers were also injured. A UN panel (the Palmer report, 2011) found Israel's naval blockade legal but the force used 'excessive and unreasonable,' and criticized the flotilla organizers . Turkey expelled Israel's ambassador

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: Apology, Compensation, and Two False Dawns
told: Turkey and Israel never tried to fix relations.
record: In March 2013 Israel apologized for the raid; a 2016 agreement included $20 million in compensation and the return of ambassadors . After Israeli forces killed dozens of protesters at the Gaza fence in May 2018, Turkey expelled Israel's ambassador. Relations were restored in 2022 with President Isaac Herzog's visit to Ankara; Turkey's new ambassador, Şakir Özkan Torunlar, took up his post in October 2022 — the first since 2018 — and was recalled in October 2023 .

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: After October 7 — Hamas Hosted, an Ambassador Recalled, Ties 'Severed'
told: Turkey either fully broke with Israel or did nothing at all.
record: Unlike Israel, the US and the EU, Turkey has never designated Hamas a terrorist organization, and its leaders have operated from Turkey . Turkey recalled its ambassador in October 2023 . On November 13, 2024, returning from Saudi Arabia and Azerbaijan, Erdoğan said Turkey had 'severed all relations' with Israel and pointed to a UN arms-embargo initiative backed by 52 countries . Yet diplomatic relations formally continued, and economic links persisted in some channels (next scene) .

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: The Oil Kept Flowing — Trade Cut, Airspace Closed, Azerbaijani Crude Still Crossing Turkey
told: Turkey's boycott of Israel is total.
record: Turkey suspended trade with Israel in 2024 and later closed its airspace and ports to Israel . Analysts note that Azerbaijani oil transiting Turkey to Israel continued unaffected even amid rising tensions, and that allegations surfaced of trade by businesses linked to Erdoğan's family after October 7 . Azerbaijan is among Israel's largest crude suppliers, and its oil reaches the Mediterranean through Turkey (see the planned Azerbaijan chapter).

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: Turkey in the Courts — The ICJ Case and 37 Istanbul Warrants
told: Turkey's legal actions are either pure justice or pure politics.
record: Turkey joined South Africa's ICJ genocide case in 2024 . On November 7, 2025 the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office announced arrest warrants for 37 people under Turkish law allowing prosecution of crimes abroad, naming among others Netanyahu, Defense Minister Israel Katz, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, and citing the bombing of the Turkish-built Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital in Gaza . Israel rejected the move; Israeli officials and critics noted that the same prosecutor's office had detained Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, Erdoğan's m

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: Rivals Over Syria — Turkey's Client, Israel's Strikes
told: Syria is only an Israel–Syria issue.
record: Turkey supported the opposition that toppled Assad and backs Syria's new government; Syrian sources say Turkey has pressed al-Sharaa on regional files . Israel, which seized a buffer zone in southern Syria and has struck across the country (see the Israel–Syria chapter), has opposed a Turkish military presence there; pro-Israel analysts describe Turkey as building a 'ring of fire' around Israel . Asked in June 2026 whether Israel and Turkey might clash, President Trump said, 'I don't think that will happen with Turkey' .

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: 2026 — Rhetoric at a Peak, Two Elections, and the Question Nobody Wants to Ask
told: Israel–Turkey relations are stable.
record: In spring 2026 Erdoğan accused Israel of atrocities in Gaza and Lebanon, and Israeli minister Amichai Eliyahu vowed to propose severing diplomatic ties . The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a pro-Israel think tank, argued that Turkey's posture was moving toward implicit military threats . A September 2026 essay in Mosaic predicted further deterioration if Netanyahu won the October 2026 election . Status as of October 7, 2026: diplomatic relations formally exist, ambassadors are absent, trade is suspended, and the two states are rivals in Syria.

chapter_name: Israel-Turkey Architecture — From the Sultan's 'No' to the Istanbul Warrants
title: The Machine in Code — One Object, Two Protocols
told: A country's stated policy is its policy.
record: Plainly: Turkey tells the world it has cut Israel off, and in key ways it has — trade, airspace, courts. But the oil that matters to both economies keeps moving across Turkish soil. Two faces of the same state, each visible to a different audience.

chapter_name: Israel-Yemen Architecture — The Houthis and the 'Proxy' Frame
title: On Eagles' Wings — The Airlift of Yemen's Jews
told: Yemen's connection to Israel begins with the Houthis.
record: Between June 1949 and September 1950 Operation Magic Carpet airlifted about 49,000 Yemeni Jews to Israel, organized with the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee and flown by Alaska Airlines and other carriers; many walked for weeks to reach Aden . The community had lived in Yemen for well over a thousand years. In Israel many were placed in transit camps, where hundreds of children were reported dead or vanished — the 'Yemenite Children Affair,' for which Israel expressed 'regret' and paid compensation in 2021 (see 'The Yemenite Children Affair').

chapter_name: Israel-Yemen Architecture — The Houthis and the 'Proxy' Frame
title: Who the Houthis Are — A Zaydi Revival, Six Wars With Yemen's Government, and the Capital in 2014
told: The Houthis are an Iranian creation built to attack Israel.
record: The movement, formally Ansar Allah, emerged in the 1990s from a Zaydi religious revival in Saada province under Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi, opposing President Ali Abdullah Saleh's government and Saudi-influenced Salafism . Its slogan — 'God is great, death to America, death to Israel, curse on the Jews, victory to Islam' — dates from the early 2000s; the 'curse on the Jews' line is antisemitic on its face . It fought six wars with the Yemeni government between 2004 and 2010 (Hussein al-Houthi was killed in 2004) , and in September 2014 took Sanaa . Iranian support grew over the following deca

chapter_name: Israel-Yemen Architecture — The Houthis and the 'Proxy' Frame
title: The War Before This War — The Saudi-Led Coalition, and ~377,000 Dead
told: The Houthis' conflict is mainly with Israel.
record: Saudi Arabia launched its intervention in March 2015 to restore the internationally recognized government; the coalition drew on US and UK weapons, refueling and intelligence . A UN-commissioned estimate put deaths by the end of 2021 at about 377,000, most from indirect causes such as hunger and disease . A truce in April 2022 produced a de facto halt between the coalition and the Houthis for years .

chapter_name: Israel-Yemen Architecture — The Houthis and the 'Proxy' Frame
title: Gaza Becomes Their Cause — 130+ Missiles at Israel, 100+ Ships Attacked
told: Houthi attacks were random terrorism unconnected to Gaza.
record: The Houthi leader warned on October 10, 2023 and the group formally announced entry into the war on October 31 . Its stated aim at sea was to stop the bombing of Gaza and force aid into the Strip . In total it launched over 130 ballistic missiles and dozens of drones at Israel — one killed a civilian in Tel Aviv in July 2024, prompting Israel's first strike in Yemen — and attacked more than 100 merchant vessels, sinking two and killing four sailors . The US and UK began strikes in January 2024 . The attacks on civilian shipping are widely described as violations of international law .

chapter_name: Israel-Yemen Architecture — The Houthis and the 'Proxy' Frame
title: Israel and the US Strike Back — Hodeidah, Sanaa, a Prime Minister Killed, and a US Deal That Excluded Israel
told: The US and Israel fought the Houthis as one.
record: Israel carried out strikes in July, September and December 2024 and through 2025 on Hodeidah port, power plants and Sanaa ; an August 24, 2025 strike on Sanaa killed 10 and wounded 102, and on August 28 Israel killed the Houthi-led government's prime minister, Ahmed al-Rahawi . The US ran a major air campaign from March to May 2025; on May 6 President Trump announced the Houthis had agreed to stop attacking ships, and the Houthis stressed the ceasefire did not apply to Israel 'in any way, shape, or form' . The Houthis also detained dozens of UN staff in 2025 .

chapter_name: Israel-Yemen Architecture — The Houthis and the 'Proxy' Frame
title: The Pause Test — Do the Houthis Follow Gaza or Tehran?
told: Either 'the Houthis are pure Iranian puppets' or 'they act only for Gaza.'
record: Two documented patterns sit side by side. First, the Houthis halted attacks on Israel during the Gaza ceasefires of January–March 2025 and October 2025–March 2026  — behavior that tracks Gaza. Second, after the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, 2026, the Houthis threatened to join and, on March 28, resumed missile attacks on Israel 'in coordination with Hezbollah and Iran,' reportedly after pressure from both; attacks paused under the Iran-war ceasefire (the Islamabad Memorandum) . The record therefore supports a mixed reading: a movement with its own motives that also acts as part o

chapter_name: Israel-Yemen Architecture — The Houthis and the 'Proxy' Frame
title: The 'Proxy' Frame — Does the Same Blame Pattern Apply to Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis?
told: All three are simply Iranian proxies with no causes of their own.
record: The frame: Israeli leaders have described Iran as the head of an 'octopus' whose arms include Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis, and analysts speak of a 'ring of fire' (see the Turkey chapter). What supports it: Iran has funded, armed or trained all three, and in 2026 the Houthis and Hezbollah fought in coordination with Iran (previous scene; see 'Two Fathers'). chapter_name: Israel-Yemen Architecture — The Houthis and the 'Proxy' Frame
title: 2026 — Joining Iran's War, Blockading Saudi Oil, and the Old Civil War Reigniting
told: With Israel quiet, the Houthis are inactive.
record: After joining the Iran war in March 2026 , the Houthis announced a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia on July 20 and attacked Saudi tankers, including one off Yanbu, Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea oil port, in August . Saudi Arabia announced a new international alliance to guard the Red Sea; Houthi strikes on Abha airport in July threatened to reignite the civil war . In early October Yemeni government forces claimed 257 strikes on Houthi positions and at least 700 fighters killed — a claim not independently verified . Status as of October 7, 2026.

told: If they act alike, they are the same thing.
record: Plainly: three groups can coordinate with Iran without being the same group or having the same cause. Looking only at what they share — the protocol — hides where each came from — the superclass.

chapter_name: Israel-UAE Architecture — The Accords, the Arms, and an Iron Dome on Arab Soil
title: Before the Handshake — A Hotel Assassination in Dubai, and Quiet Ties
told: Israel and the UAE had no relationship before 2020.
record: On January 19, 2010 Mahmoud al-Mabhouh, a Hamas military commander, was killed in his Dubai hotel room; Dubai police released CCTV footage and identified a team of more than two dozen suspects travelling on forged or fraudulently used European and Australian passports, and blamed Mossad, which Israel neither confirmed nor denied . Several governments expelled Israeli diplomats over the passports. Quiet contacts nonetheless grew, and in 2015 Israel opened a mission accredited to the International Renewable Energy Agency in Abu Dhabi — its first official presence in the UAE .

chapter_name: Israel-UAE Architecture — The Accords, the Arms, and an Iron Dome on Arab Soil
title: The Abraham Accords — Normalization in Exchange for Shelving Annexation
told: The UAE normalized with Israel with nothing asked in return.
record: The normalization agreement was announced on August 13, 2020 and signed on September 15 at the White House, alongside Bahrain ; the UAE was the first Arab country in 26 years to normalize relations with Israel . The UAE presented suspension of Israel's annexation plans as the condition and justification; Emirati officials later said this was an actual, not just public, rationale . Israeli officials have since said that commitment was time-limited; Emirati officials say annexation would violate the spirit of the accords . Morocco and Sudan followed in late 2020.

chapter_name: Israel-UAE Architecture — The Accords, the Arms, and an Iron Dome on Arab Soil
title: The Other Price — F-35s, a $23 Billion Arms Package, and Why It Stalled
told: The accords were purely about peace, with no arms component.
record: Following the accords, the US announced a roughly $23 billion arms package for the UAE, including F-35 fighters, MQ-9 Reaper drones and munitions . US law requires preserving Israel's 'qualitative military edge,' and Israel had long opposed F-35s for Arab states; the sale moved forward after normalization . In December 2021 the UAE suspended talks on the F-35s, citing US technical and operational conditions . Israeli arms exports also grew: Bahrain and the UAE bought nearly $900 million in Israeli arms in 2021 .

chapter_name: Israel-UAE Architecture — The Accords, the Arms, and an Iron Dome on Arab Soil
title: Pegasus in the Emirates — A Jailed Activist and a Leaked List
told: Israeli technology sales to the UAE were purely commercial and benign.
record: In August 2016 the Citizen Lab and Lookout documented an attempt to infect Ahmed Mansoor's iPhone with NSO Group's Pegasus via a malicious link — the case that first exposed Pegasus publicly; Mansoor was arrested in 2017 and sentenced in 2018 to ten years in prison . The 2021 Pegasus Project consortium of news organizations identified the UAE among suspected Pegasus clients based on a leaked list of phone numbers . Sales of NSO's software abroad require export licenses from Israel's Defense Ministry (see 'Unit 8200 and the NSA').

chapter_name: Israel-UAE Architecture — The Accords, the Arms, and an Iron Dome on Arab Soil
title: Trade, Flights and Tech — The Civilian Side of Normalization
told: Normalization produced nothing tangible.
record: The two countries signed a comprehensive economic partnership agreement in 2022 . Goods trade exceeded $3.2 billion in 2024, excluding government-to-government deals, software and services . After October 7 the UAE condemned Hamas's attack and kept flights to Israel operating from the first day of the war, when nearly all other carriers suspended service .

chapter_name: Israel-UAE Architecture — The Accords, the Arms, and an Iron Dome on Arab Soil
title: Through the Gaza War — Condemnation, Airdrops, Criticism, and No Break
told: The UAE either abandoned Palestinians or broke with Israel.
record: Abu Dhabi condemned the October 7 attack and maintained relations throughout the war, using them to coordinate air drops of aid into Gaza and working with the Israeli government on a post-war plan . It also criticized Israel's conduct in Gaza and the West Bank . Critics argue that no Abraham Accords state 'even suggested leaving' despite the war, and that the accords provided political cover ; supporters argue continued engagement delivered aid and gave the UAE leverage, as in 2025 (next scene) .

told: The Abraham Accords kept the UAE out of the region's wars.

Israel deployed an Iron Dome battery and several dozen troops to operate it early in the war — the first operational use of the system outside Israel and the US — and Israeli aircraft struck short-range missile launchers in southern Iran to protect the Gulf . The Wall Street Journal reported the UAE carri

chapter_name: Israel-UAE Architecture — The Accords, the Arms, and an Iron Dome on Arab Soil
title: What Normalization Delivered — and to Whom
told: Either 'the accords brought peace' or 'they brought nothing.'
record: Documented gains: a free-trade agreement and $3.2 billion+ in annual goods trade; direct flights that continued through the war; arms sales in both directions; Israeli air defense in the UAE in 2026; and, by Emirati account, the suspension of annexation in 2020 and its deferral after the September 2025 red-line warning . Documented limits: no movement toward a Palestinian state, surveillance exports used against a jailed activist, and — as critics stress — no signatory has suspended the accords despite the Gaza war . Supporters call the accords' endurance through war their proof; critics call

chapter_name: Israel-UAE Architecture — The Accords, the Arms, and an Iron Dome on Arab Soil
title: The Machine in Code — Everything Retained Strongly Except the Stated Reason
told: The accords exist to advance a Palestinian state.
record: Plainly: when a deal's concrete parts — money, weapons, protection — are locked in, and its stated purpose is not, the purpose can disappear without the deal changing at all. That is a weak reference.

chapter_name: The Other Accords — Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan
title: Each Paid in a Different Coin — How the Other Accords Were Bought
told: Arab states joined the Abraham Accords spontaneously, out of a change of heart.
record: Bahrain signed with the UAE at the White House on September 15, 2020 . In a December 2020 joint declaration Morocco and Israel agreed to normalize and the United States became the first country to recognize Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara; that same month the US removed Sudan from its State Sponsors of Terrorism list, and in January 2021 Sudan signed the Accords declaration . Kazakhstan, which already had full relations with Israel, announced its accession in November 2025 . In May 2026 President Trump suggested Israel's neighbors should be required to join as part of a peace deal in

chapter_name: The Other Accords — Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan
title: Bahrain — The Fifth Fleet's Host, a Recalled Ambassador, and a Quiet Cooling
told: Bahrain's normalization proceeded without friction.
record: The US Fifth Fleet has been headquartered in Bahrain since 1995 . Bahrain signed the Accords on September 15, 2020 . In November 2023 Bahrain's parliament announced that Israel's ambassador had left and Bahrain's ambassador had been recalled, and that economic ties were halted; the government confirmed the ambassadors' departure . Analysts describe Bahrain's relations as having cooled, but Bahrain has not left the Accords , and its ambassador attended the US-hosted sixth-anniversary gathering in September 2026 .

chapter_name: The Other Accords — Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan
title: Morocco Before the Accords — An Ancient Jewish Community, a Paid Emigration, and Offices Opened Then Closed
told: Morocco–Israel ties began in 2020.
record: Morocco's Jewish community, rooted over two millennia and numbering in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s, largely emigrated after 1948, mostly to Israel. Between 1961 and 1964 Operation Yachin brought about 97,000 Moroccan Jews to Israel; historians record that Israel, with American Jewish organizations, made payments to the Moroccan government to allow the departures . Israelis of Moroccan descent became one of Israel's largest communities. Morocco and Israel opened low-level liaison offices in 1994 after Oslo and closed them in 2000 amid the second intifada .

chapter_name: The Other Accords — Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan
title: Western Sahara — The Price of Morocco's Normalization
told: Normalization with Morocco was free of third-party costs.
record: Morocco took control of most of Western Sahara after Spain's withdrawal in 1975; the Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, seeks independence, and the UN has long listed the territory as non-self-governing . The December 2020 US–Morocco–Israel declaration paired normalization with US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty — the first by any country ; Israel later recognized it as well . A UN resolution in late 2025 supported Morocco's autonomy proposal as a basis for a settlement , while the territory's final status remains unresolved at the UN .

chapter_name: The Other Accords — Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan
title: Morocco in 2026 — Full Embassies, Protests at Home, and Security Ties That Never Stopped
told: Moroccan public opinion supports normalization.
record: Foreign Ministers Nasser Bourita and Gideon Sa'ar, hosted by US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, agreed on September 16, 2026 to elevate missions to embassies and appoint ambassadors, restore direct flights by carriers from both countries before the end of 2026, and finalize investment-protection and double-taxation agreements . The US and Israel reaffirmed support for Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and the autonomy plan as 'the only serious and credible basis' to end the dispute . Reestablishing relations sparked protests and opposition among many Moroccans during the Gaza war ; def

chapter_name: The Other Accords — Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan
title: Sudan — From the Capital of the 'Three No's' to a Secret Meeting in Uganda
told: Sudan was always hostile to Israel, or always open to it.
record: The Arab League summit in Khartoum in August–September 1967 adopted the resolution remembered for its 'three no's': no peace with Israel, no recognition, no negotiations . After the 2019 fall of Omar al-Bashir, the transitional leader Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan met Netanyahu in Entebbe, Uganda, in February 2020 . Normalization was announced in October 2020 .

chapter_name: The Other Accords — Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan
title: Sudan's Unratified Accord — A Terrorism Delisting, a Coup, and a War
told: Sudan is a full Abraham Accords member with normal relations with Israel.
record: The US delisted Sudan as a state sponsor of terrorism in December 2020, and Sudan signed the Abraham Accords Declaration in January 2021 ; the agreement has remained unratified . The military took full control in an October 2021 coup, and in April 2023 war broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces, causing one of the world's largest humanitarian crises . Analysts describe Sudan's formalization as stalled by internal instability .

chapter_name: The Other Accords — Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan
title: The Ledger — What Each Country Got, and What Their Publics Got
told: Normalization reflected the will of each country's people.
record: Each government's reward was concrete: recognition of a territorial claim (Morocco), removal from the terrorism list (Sudan), deepened US security ties (Bahrain), and diplomatic standing (Kazakhstan) . Normalization was decided by monarchs or military rulers; no public referendum or ratification by an elected legislature occurred in Bahrain, Morocco or Sudan. Protests followed in Morocco and Bahrain during the Gaza war . None of the signatories has formally left the Accords .

chapter_name: The Other Accords — Bahrain, Morocco, Sudan and Kazakhstan
title: The Machine in Code — Same Selector, Different Argument
told: Each country normalized for peace.
record: Plainly: headlines said four more countries made peace with Israel. Each actually made a trade with Washington, and the thing traded was different every time — land, a list, protection, prestige.

chapter_name: Israel-Azerbaijan Architecture — Oil for Arms, and the Pipeline Across Turkey
title: Iran's Northern Neighbor — Why Israel Courted a Shia-Majority Republic
told: Israel's partners in the Muslim world are only Arab states that signed peace deals.
record: Relations date to Azerbaijan's independence in the early 1990s, when Israel sought a counter to Iran on its northern border . Azerbaijan is Shia-majority but governed as a secular state; Iran is home to an estimated 20 million ethnic Azerbaijanis, whom President Aliyev has called 'compatriots' . Baku long avoided a formal embassy in Israel to avoid alienating Muslim states; after its 2020 victory over Armenia it opened one in Tel Aviv in 2023 .

chapter_name: Israel-Azerbaijan Architecture — Oil for Arms, and the Pipeline Across Turkey
title: The Oil — 40 to 60 Percent of Israel's Crude, Through a Pipeline Across Turkey
told: Israel's oil comes mainly from distant global markets with no political strings.
record: Azerbaijan's crude has accounted for between 40 and 60 percent of Israel's oil in recent years ; in early 2026 the share of Israel's oil imports arriving through the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline reached 46% . The BTC pipeline, opened in 2006, runs from the Caspian through Georgia to Ceyhan on Turkey's Mediterranean coast . Baku did not suspend shipments during the Gaza war . Azerbaijan's state oil company SOCAR also took a 10% stake in Israel's Tamar gas field and joined exploration in Israeli waters .

chapter_name: Israel-Azerbaijan Architecture — Oil for Arms, and the Pipeline Across Turkey
title: The Arms — About 69 Percent of Azerbaijan's Major Weapons From Israel
told: Azerbaijan's military buildup was independent of Israel.
record: According to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute data, Israel supplied about 69% of Azerbaijan's major arms imports in 2016–2021, with nearly 100 Israeli arms flights landing in Baku in that period ; other analyses cite 60–70% . US arms sales to Azerbaijan have been restricted since 1992 under Section 907 of the Freedom Support Act, which has made Israel's role larger .

chapter_name: Israel-Azerbaijan Architecture — Oil for Arms, and the Pipeline Across Turkey
title: Nagorno-Karabakh — Israeli Weapons, Two Wars, and 100,000 Armenians Gone in a Week
told: Israel's arms sales to Azerbaijan had no humanitarian consequence.
record: Israel played a key role in Azerbaijan's defeat of Armenia in 2020 and 2023 . AP reported that Israel supplied powerful weapons to Azerbaijan in the weeks before the September 19, 2023 offensive; Armenia's ambassador to Israel said Israeli weapons were 'firing at our people,' and Israel's foreign and defense ministries declined to comment . After a nine-month blockade of the only road to Armenia, the offensive forced the enclave's authorities to capitulate in two days; over 100,000 ethnic Armenians — about 85% of the population within a week — fled, and Armenia's government called it ethnic cl

chapter_name: Israel-Azerbaijan Architecture — Oil for Arms, and the Pipeline Across Turkey
title: Lobbying Washington Through Israel's Friends — AIPAC in Baku and a Trilateral Pitch
told: Azerbaijan's US relations are separate from Israel.
record: Section 907 restricts direct US aid and arms sales to Azerbaijan . In December 2024 AIPAC leaders Michael Tuchin and Bernie Kaminetsky made their first visit to Baku and assured President Aliyev that 'your support for Israel will be recognised' . Netanyahu's office announced Israel seeks to 'establish a strong foundation for trilateral collaboration' with the US and Azerbaijan, and analysts describe Azerbaijan as a potential Abraham Accords candidate — though it already has full relations with Israel .

chapter_name: Israel-Azerbaijan Architecture — Oil for Arms, and the Pipeline Across Turkey

chapter_name: Israel-Ethiopia — Rescue, and What Came After
title: Beta Israel — An Ancient Community, and the Ruling That Made Them Eligible
told: Ethiopian Jews were always welcomed by Israel as Jews.
record: The Beta Israel ('House of Israel') lived for centuries in the Gondar and Tigray regions, practicing a Judaism distinct from rabbinic tradition . Their status was disputed by Israel's religious authorities until 1973, when Sephardi Chief Rabbi Ovadia Yosef recognized them as Jews; the government applied the Law of Return in 1975 . Even then, in 1985 the chief rabbinate required a symbolic conversion ritual before accepting them fully . By the end of 2019 about 155,300 Ethiopian Jews lived in Israel .

chapter_name: Israel-Ethiopia — Rescue, and What Came After
title: The Trek and Operation Moses — 8,000 Flown Out, About 4,000 Dead on the Way
told: The Ethiopian airlifts were publicity events staged for the cameras.
record: Beta Israel walked to Sudan's camps, where many died of disease and hunger; estimates of the dead range from about 2,000 to 5,000, and the community commemorates 4,000 . Operation Moses airlifted about 8,000 people between November 21, 1984 and January 5, 1985, with Sudanese and CIA cooperation . It ended prematurely after a press leak in Israel, when Sudan's Arab allies pressured Khartoum to stop the flights . Hundreds were left behind.

chapter_name: Israel-Ethiopia — Rescue, and What Came After
title: Operation Joshua and the Long Wait — A US Airlift, Then Six Years

record: Vice President Bush arranged Operation Joshua (also called Operation Sheba), in which the US Air Force flew the 494 Beta Israel remaining in Sudan to Israel in 1985 . Between Operations Moses/Joshua and 1991, only a small number of Ethiopian Jews were able to leave Africa .

chapter_name: Israel-Ethiopia — Rescue, and What Came After

record: Operation Solomon, overseen by Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, transported 14,325 Beta Israel to Israel in 36 hours on May 24–25, 1991; American diplomats helped negotiate with the collapsing Ethiopian government, and the American Association for Ethiopian Jews pressed for faster action . Planes were packed far beyond normal capacity.
